title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 4: Paradigms Change But Values Endure
keywords: DNA, surrogate parenthood and human cloning
primary_topics: Chapter 4 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's commencement address to the graduates of the University of the East, arguing that although the megashift to the information age will remake every career, the answer is not new theories but old values, because 'paradigms change but values endure.'

His survey of the e-age itself -- Naisbitt's 'megashift' from an industrial community to an information society, the new e-age fortunes of Gates, Morgridge and Chambers, Moore and Noyce, Bezos, Case, Dell and Schwab, and Bill Gates's forecast in 'The Road Ahead' of a wallet-sized computer that replaces money, camera, map and phone.

The concrete effect of that shift on the graduates' professions -- radically amended court procedures and rules of evidence, new doctrines for e-commerce, deregulation, privatization and liberalization, painless dentistry, and the 1.6 million new 'infotech' jobs Ambassador Maceda reported for that year.

His prescription of three enduring values summarized as the three Es and the acronym ExEE -- excellence (developing to the maximum whatever gift one was given, illustrated by 3M's Art Fry and the Post It note), ethics (character ethic, and 'a change in men' rather than a change of men), and eternity (life after death, faith in a God who provides in His own time and His own way).
sub_topics: He opened by thanking UE president Dr. Josefina R. Cortes and Law Dean Carlos M. Ortega, recalling that although he finished law at neighboring FEU, UE was the site of the 1960 bar examinations in which he was one of the topnotchers.

He recalled nearly missing those examinations after falling ill, walking over knee-deep flood water from the FEU Hospital to the UE gate, and credited his dean Dr. Jovito R. Salonga for urging him to go on in spite of illness and misfortune.
He congratulated the graduates as 'millennial graduates' finishing at the turn of the century, and felicitated the parents who, like his own, sacrificed hard-earned money for quality education.

He explained the megashift using Naisbitt's 'Megatrends' and Drucker -- prosperity now depends on the processing, possession and distribution of information, and the central workforce of the knowledge society will be highly specialized people.

He contrasted the old icons of industry (Rockefeller, Vanderbilt, Ford) with the new e-age pioneers -- Gates of Microsoft, Morgridge and Chambers of Cisco, Moore and Noyce of Intel, Bezos of Amazon.com, Case, Dell and Schwab.

Drawing on 'The Road Ahead,' he described a wallet-sized computer replacing money, credit card, checkbook, address book, camera, TV, cellular phone, map, compass and even a loud whistle to summon help.

He applied the change to the professions: rules of evidence and court procedure to be amended radically, new doctrines for electronic commerce and for deregulation, privatization and liberalization, and DNA, surrogate parenthood and cloning altering civil and criminal law.

He illustrated change in dentistry through Dr. Rufino Achacoso, whose pedal-powered drills once frayed his nerves but who now works painlessly, and cited Ambassador Ernesto M. Maceda on 1.6 million new infotech jobs, more than half open to non-Americans.
Against that background he gave what he conceded sounded strange advice -- to retain, practise and internalize old values, summarized as three Es and the acronym ExEE.

On excellence, he argued that everyone must develop to the maximum whatever natural gift the Lord gave, that excellence need not come with Latin honors, and told the story of 3M employee Art Fry, whose choir hymn markers led to the Post It note and a $300 million business.
He urged a passion for excellence beyond formal schooling, noting that CD-ROMs and the Internet teach faster than passive books or occasional lectures, and that learning must not stop at graduation.

On ethics, he traced professional codes and canons to character ethic -- integrity, humility, fidelity, courage, prudence and hard work -- and insisted that to change society what is needed is a change in men, not merely a change of men.
He dismissed motivational speeches and quick-fix solutions as Band Aid and aspirin, quoting Emerson that what you are shouts so loudly that your words cannot be heard.
On eternity, he assured the graduates of life after death and of a God amongst, above, before, beside, behind and within them, quoting Isaiah that God's thoughts and ways are higher than ours.
In his epilogue he summarized the address and imagined a graduate telling his children decades later that he succeeded because on graduation day he heard, believed and practised the ExEE message.

stances.claim: New paradigms are best met not by new theories but by old values, because 'paradigms change but values endure.'
stances.rhetorical_move: counterintuitive turn: after pages of futurism he tells graduates his advice will sound strange, then prescribes the old

stances.claim: Excellence is everyone's duty because each person must develop to the maximum whatever natural gift he was given, and it can be reached by the most ordinary graduate.
stances.rhetorical_move: example-driven proof: the ordinary 3M employee Art Fry whose choir problem became the Post It note and a $300 million business

stances.claim: To reform society and government what is needed is a change in men, not just a change of men, since ethical values must be internalized from inside the heart.
stances.rhetorical_move: aphoristic inversion backed by Emerson and a triad of impossibilities (swindler, chatterbox, atheist)

stances.claim: Life on earth is not the only life; there is an eternity where our final destiny lies, and God provides what is good for us in His own time and His own way.
stances.rhetorical_move: faith assurance closed with Scripture from Isaiah

notable_anecdotes: He nearly missed the 1960 bar examinations: confined at the FEU Hospital days before the first test, he walked over knee-deep flood water on R. Papa Street to the UE gate during a typhoon, encouraged by Dean Jovito R. Salonga to sit the exams in spite of illness and misfortune.

As a teenager he dreaded the clinic of the then young dentist Rufino Achacoso, whose pedal-powered drills frayed his nerves; he still sees the graying Dr. Achacoso, who now bores molars and implants teeth without pain.
He told of Art Fry, an ordinary 3M employee whose church hymn markers kept falling out of the books, leading him to propose the adhesive-backed yellow paper now known as the Post It note pad.

He closed by imagining a graduate twenty or thirty years on telling his children that he succeeded because on his graduation day he heard, believed and practised the three Es from his commencement speaker.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' reproduced CJP's commencement address at the University of the East, in which he told the graduates that the world they were entering had already undergone what John Naisbitt called a 'megashift' from an industrial community to an information society, where prosperity depends on the processing, possession and distribution of information and where, as Drucker wrote, the central workforce would consist of highly specialized people. He opened by thanking UE president Josefina R. Cortes and Law Dean Carlos M. Ortega, recalling that although he studied law at FEU, UE was the site of the 1960 bar examinations in which he placed among the topnotchers, and that he had nearly missed those examinations after falling ill, walking through knee-deep floodwater from the FEU Hospital at the urging of his dean, Jovito R. Salonga. He then catalogued the new e-age fortunes -- Gates, Morgridge and Chambers, Moore and Noyce, Bezos, Case, Dell and Schwab -- and, drawing on Gates's 'The Road Ahead,' described a wallet-sized computer that would replace money, camera, phone and map. He warned that the shift would reshape the graduates' careers: rules of evidence and court procedure would be radically amended, electronic commerce and deregulation would require new doctrines, DNA and cloning would alter civil and criminal law, dentistry would be transformed, and 1.6 million new infotech jobs were opening. His advice, he conceded, would sound strange: to meet new paradigms the graduates should retain, practise and internalize old values, because paradigms change but values endure. He summarized these as three Es under the acronym ExEE -- excellence, illustrated by the 3M employee Art Fry whose Post It note grew from a choir problem; ethics, rooted in character ethic and requiring a change in men rather than a change of men; and eternity, the life after death where our final destiny lies -- closing with Isaiah and an imagined graduate crediting his success decades later to that day's message.
